To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the aging face is a complex process that is best treated with multiple, complementary techniques that address the various components of the aging face.

the aging process of the face is characterized by the loss of facial volume, which occurs preferentially in certain compartments, and that these compartments can be augmented with injectable materials to restore facial volume.
the face can be divided into superficial and deep fat compartments, which are partitioned by discrete fascial barriers and are affected by aging in a specific and predictable manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the anatomic changes that occur in the face during the aging process and the implications of those changes on surgical treatment.
identifying the specific fat compartments of facial aging and their role in facial rejuvenation.
the anatomic and physiologic aspects of the aging face, and how this knowledge can be translated into a rational approach to facial rejuvenative surgery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
facial aging is a complex process that is multifactorial, and that the facial skeleton and soft tissue envelope undergo significant changes.
a precise knowledge of the facial fat compartments and their age-related volumetric changes is essential for successful and predictable results in facial rejuvenation.
the aging face has a predictable pattern of fat loss that is site-specific and can be addressed with site-specific augmentation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the superficial fat compartments of the midface are best treated with fillers and the deep fat compartments of the cheek are best treated with autologous fat grafting.
the face can be divided into superficial and deep fat compartments.
facial aging is the result of a complex interplay of volume loss in the deep facial fat compartments and laxity in the overlying soft tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the face is not a single entity but is comprised of multiple independent units, each with its own unique aging process.
the superficial fat compartments are not static and that they are dynamic structures that undergo age-related changes.
the superficial fat compartment of the face can be augmented with hyaluronic acid fillers and that this can be performed with excellent safety and efficacy.
